purpose: The ways a running typescript program can HOLD layer-1 content. Not layer 1 (the data is fixed), not layer 3 (no operations beyond load-and-read-back), not the type system.
reference: language knowledge, checked against ../type_vocabulary/raw/typescript.types.json as a candidate checklist only (superseded node; not a decision instrument).

nothing.note: the value representing a deliberate absence.
the value a variable holds before assignment; a second absence value distinct from null.
the type used for absence of a return value; under strict null checks the only value assignable to it is undefined.

truth.note: two values, no numeric side at the type level (though javascript coerces underneath).

whole.note: IEEE double; every plain integer literal is parsed into this holder, exact only up to 2^53 (the p53_plus1 and u64max edges erode).
arbitrary-precision integer, a holder separate from number; compiled with --target es2020 so the n-suffixed literal is legal.

fractional.note: IEEE double, the sole fractional holder typescript offers.

text.note: a run of utf-16 code units presented as text; the default text holder.
split by unicode codepoint via the string iterator, not by utf-16 code unit; recovers the clef as one element instead of a surrogate pair.
holds text only as encoded utf-8 bytes; the codepoints are gone until decoded.

sequence.note: growable ordered run; element kind widens to unknown/any when the values differ.
fixed length and a declared kind per position, checked at compile time; reassigning an element refuses under readonly.

probes.mixed: const v: readonly [number, string, number, boolean, null] = [1, "two", 3.0, true, null];

sequence.note: unordered, no duplicates; kept in the table because that loss is the finding.

probes.mixed: let v: Set<unknown> = new Set([1, "two", 3.0, true, null]);

sequence.note: fixed-width 32-bit signed integer elements; every value is coerced through ToInt32, so overflow and non-numeric input wrap or zero out silently instead of refusing.

probes.strs: let v: Int32Array = new Int32Array(["a", "b"] as any);
probes.mixed: let v: Int32Array = new Int32Array([1, "two", 3.0, true, null] as any);
probes.bigint: let v: Int32Array = new Int32Array([9223372036854775808] as any);

sequence.note: fixed-width 64-bit holder built from bigint elements; reaches exactly the i64 edges the census flags, and refuses non-bigint input at run time with a TypeError.

probes.strs: let v: BigInt64Array = new BigInt64Array(["a", "b"] as any);
probes.mixed: let v: BigInt64Array = new BigInt64Array([1n, "two" as any, 3n, true as any, null as any]);

keyed.note: name to element; the engine keeps insertion order for string keys though the index-signature type does not promise it.

probes.flat: let v: { [k: string]: number } = { a: 1, b: 2, c: 3 };
probes.nested: let v: { outer: { inner: number[] } } = { outer: { inner: [1, 2] } };

keyed.note: keys of any kind, not just strings, and guaranteed insertion order.

probes.empty: let v: Map<string, number> = new Map();
probes.flat: let v: Map<string, number> = new Map([["a", 1], ["b", 2], ["c", 3]]);
probes.emptykey: let v: Map<string, string> = new Map([["", "empty-string key"]]);
probes.nested: let v: Map<string, { inner: number[] }> = new Map([["outer", { inner: [1, 2] }]]);

keyed.note: the mapped-type spelling of the same object-literal holder; a compile-time name for the shape, not a different run-time thing.

probes.flat: const v: Record<string, number> = { a: 1, b: 2, c: 3 };
probes.nested: const v: Record<string, { inner: number[] }> = { outer: { inner: [1, 2] } };

keyed.spelling: interface Flat { a: number; b: number; c: number; } const v: Flat = { a: 1, b: 2, c: 3 };
keyed.pre:
interface Flat { a: number; b: number; c: number; }
interface Nested { outer: { inner: number[] } }
keyed.note: names fixed at compile time by a declared interface; the odd keys still fit since typescript property names may be any string or numeric literal, quoted in the object literal.

probes.flat: const v: Flat = { a: 1, b: 2, c: 3 };
probes.intlike: const v: { "1": string; b: number } = { "1": "string-one-key", b: 2 };

keyed.spelling: class Flat3 { a: number; b: number; c: number; constructor(a: number, b: number, c: number) { this.a = a; this.b = b; this.c = c; } } new Flat3(1, 2, 3)
keyed.note: names fixed when the class is declared, not when data arrives; quoted numeric and empty-string property names are legal in a class body, unlike a plain identifier.

probes.emptykey: let v: EmptyKey1 = new EmptyKey1("empty-string key");
probes.nested: let v: Nested1 = new Nested1({ inner: [1, 2] });

nesting.note: nesting by repeating the same holder; every level carries the same declared element kind unless widened.

probes.seq_in_map: let v: { outer: { inner: number[] } } = { outer: { inner: [1, 2] } };
probes.mixed_depth: let v: unknown[] = [1, [2, { k: "t" }], true, null];

nesting.note: nesting by repeating the object-literal holder; each level's fields are fixed at the point the type is written.

probes.seq_in_map: let v: { outer: { inner: number[] } } = { outer: { inner: [1, 2] } };
probes.mixed_depth: let v: { a: unknown[]; c: boolean } = { a: [1, { b: 2 }], c: true };

nesting.spelling: type Node = null | boolean | number | string | Node[] | { [k: string]: Node };
nesting.pre: type L1Node = null | boolean | number | string | L1Node[] | { [k: string]: L1Node };
nesting.note: a hand-written recursive union; the one typescript holder whose declared kind matches every layer-1 form at once, which mixed nesting needs.

probes.mixed_depth: const v: L1Node = [1, [2, { k: "t" }], true, null];

identity.note: javascript objects and arrays are held by reference, so two positions can name one object.
built by copying (spread / structuredClone) rather than referencing; the contrast cell against the reference holders — expect copied/distinct/no-cycle throughout.

identity.spelling: let v = new Map([["left", s], ["right", s]]);
identity.note: the same object reachable under two keys, an alternative shared-node holder to the array of references.
